b.x: Python is a high-level, general-purpose programming language used to create software, automate repetitive work, analyze data, build websites and APIs, and develop artificial intelligence and machine-learning applications. It is popular because its syntax is relatively readable and its ecosystem contains many reusable libraries.

A programming language lets a developer express instructions that a computer can execute through an interpreter, compiler, or runtime system. Python programs can contain variables, expressions, conditions, loops, functions, classes, and modules.
The print() function displays the supplied value. The text between quotation marks is a string. This small program illustrates Python’s readable style.

Python is often recommended to beginners because a small program can be written with little setup. However, Python is also used in large professional systems. Learning its fundamentals provides a foundation for later subjects such as functions, object-oriented programming, files, databases, APIs, data analysis, and machine learning.

sec.s: Python was created by Guido van Rossum, a Dutch programmer.

b.x: 2.1 Origins

Python was created by Guido van Rossum, a Dutch programmer. Development began in the late 1980s, and Python was first publicly released in 1991. The language was designed to be readable and practical while supporting general-purpose programming. Its design was influenced by earlier languages and programming ideas, including ABC.
The name “Python” was inspired by the comedy group Monty Python, not by the snake. This explains why Python documentation and examples have sometimes used playful names.
2.2 Python 1.x

Early Python releases established many of the language’s defining characteristics: readable syntax, high-level data structures, dynamic typing, and an interactive interpreter. These features helped programmers experiment and develop software quickly.
2.3 Python 2.x

Python 2 became a widely used generation of the language. Over time, the language needed changes that improved consistency and allowed future development. Python 3 introduced changes that were not fully compatible with Python 2, so some projects had to be updated. Official support for Python 2 ended in 2020. New learners should generally use a currently supported Python 3 version unless they need to maintain a legacy project.
2.4 Python 3 and modern development

Python 3 is the standard generation used in modern development. Successive releases have added language improvements, library features, performance changes, better tooling, and stronger support for typing and concurrency. The exact latest release changes over time, so consult official Python release information when installing Python.

Python’s popularity has grown due to its readable syntax, cross-platform support, standard library, and extensive third-party ecosystem. Data science, scientific computing, machine learning, and deep learning have further increased its use. Libraries such as NumPy, pandas, scikit-learn, PyTorch, and TensorFlow support data and AI work. Frameworks such as Django, Flask, and FastAPI support web development.

sec.s: Python is high-level because developers can work with strings, lists, dictionaries, and objects without…

b.x: 3.1 High-level language
Python is high-level because developers can work with strings, lists, dictionaries, and objects without manually controlling every low-level machine detail.
3.2 Readable syntax
Python uses indentation to define blocks of code. This makes the structure visible, but indentation is part of the language syntax rather than just a formatting preference.
The indented statement belongs to the if block.
3.3 Interpreted execution model

Python is commonly described as an interpreted language. In CPython, source code is compiled to bytecode and executed by the Python virtual machine. Most developers do not need to run a separate manual compilation step for ordinary scripts.
3.4 Dynamic typing
A variable name does not need a declared type before it can refer to a value.
This is valid because the name value can refer to an integer and later to a string. Dynamic typing is flexible, but type-related mistakes can appear at runtime.
3.5 Strong typing
Python does not automatically treat every type as interchangeable. For example, adding an integer directly to a string raises TypeError:
Explicit conversion can be used where appropriate: str(5) + “2” produces the string “52”.
3.6 Cross-platform support

Python is available for Windows, macOS, Linux, and other environments. Code using portable libraries and avoiding operating-system-specific assumptions can often run across platforms with few changes.
3.7 Standard library
Python includes modules for mathematics, files, dates, JSON, regular expressions, networking, testing, and other common tasks. This broad collection is sometimes described as “batteries included.”
3.8 Third-party packages

Packages add capabilities beyond the standard library. Examples include NumPy for numerical computing, pandas for tabular data, Matplotlib for plots, scikit-learn for machine learning, PyTorch for deep learning, and Django or Flask for web development. A third-party package may need to be installed separately, and its compatibility and security should be checked.
3.9 Multiple programming styles

Python supports procedural programming, object-oriented programming, and functional techniques. Beginners often start with variables, conditions, loops, and functions before studying classes and advanced patterns.
3.10 Automatic memory management

Python manages object memory automatically in common implementations. This reduces the need to manually allocate and free memory in ordinary programs. However, memory use can still matter for large datasets or long-running services.
3.11 Limitations

Python may be slower than some compiled languages for CPU-intensive work, depending on the task and implementation. It can still be efficient when using optimized libraries implemented in lower-level languages. Python may also be unsuitable for some strict real-time, low-level, or highly resource-constrained tasks.

Use descriptive names. total_marks is often clearer than x when calculating a student’s marks. Avoid shadowing built-in names such as list, str, or sum, because doing so can make those built-in functions unavailable under their usual names.

sec.s: A data type describes the kind of value an object represents and the operations supported by that value.

b.x: A data type describes the kind of value an object represents and the operations supported by that value. Python includes int, float, str, bool, list, tuple, dict, set, and NoneType, among other types. This chapter focuses on int, float, str, and bool.
The type() function can inspect a value’s type:
These values have types int, float, str, and bool respectively.
10.1 Integer (int)
An integer represents a whole number without a fractional part:
Python integers can grow beyond the size of a typical fixed-width machine integer, subject to available memory. They support addition, subtraction, multiplication, floor division, and modulo.
Examples: 10 + 5 produces 15. 10 - 5 produces 5. 10 * 5 produces 50. 10 // 3 produces 3. 10 % 3 produces 1.
The / operator normally produces a float, even when both operands are integers.
10.2 Floating-point number (float)
A float represents a number using binary floating-point representation:

Many decimal fractions cannot be represented exactly in binary floating point. As a result, 0.1 + 0.2 may display a result close to, but not exactly, 0.3. This is normal for binary floating-point arithmetic. For exact decimal money calculations, Python’s decimal module may be more appropriate.
10.3 String (str)
A string is a sequence of text characters. Strings can use single or double quotes:
Triple quotes can create multiline strings. Strings are immutable: operations that appear to change a string create a new string rather than modifying the original string object in place.
Common string operations
String indexes start at zero. Accessing a nonexistent index raises IndexError. Slicing is more forgiving and commonly returns the available portion of a string.
10.4 Boolean (bool)
A Boolean represents one of two truth values: True or False. Capitalization matters.
Booleans are commonly produced by comparisons

In Python, bool is a subclass of int, so True behaves like 1 and False like 0 in some contexts. For readable code, use Boolean values to express conditions rather than relying unnecessarily on numeric behavior.
10.5 None
None represents the absence of a value or a missing result in many contexts:
None is different from 0, False, and an empty string. Check it using:
The is operator checks object identity and is the customary way to compare with None.

sec.s: Type conversion changes a value from one type to another.

b.x: 11.1 Meaning

Type conversion changes a value from one type to another. It may be explicit, using functions such as int(), float(), str(), and bool(), or occur automatically in certain operations. “Type casting” is often used informally to mean explicit conversion.
11.2 Convert to int
int() converts suitable values to integers
Converting a float to int truncates the fractional part toward zero. Thus int(7.9) is 7 and int(-7.9) is -7. It does not round to the nearest integer.
int(“7.9”) raises ValueError because the string is not an integer-form string accepted by int().
11.3 Convert to float
float() converts suitable numbers and numeric strings:
An invalid numeric string raises ValueError.
11.4 Convert to str
str() creates a string representation
This can help combine text and numbers:
An f-string is often clearer
11.5 Convert to bool

bool() returns True or False according to Python’s truth-value rules. Common false values include False, None, numeric zero, empty strings, and empty containers such as [], {}, and (). Many other values are true.
A common surprise is bool(“False”) returning True. The value is a non-empty string; Python does not interpret the word inside the string as a Boolean literal.
11.6 Input and conversion
input() reads user input and returns a string:
If the user enters 18, the program prints 19. If the user enters non-numeric text, int() raises ValueError. Robust programs can use try/except to handle invalid input.
11.7 Loss of information

int(4.8) produces 4, losing the fractional part. Converting a precise decimal to float may lose precision. Converting a number to a string changes its type, so arithmetic requires converting it back. Always choose a conversion suitable for the task.

sec.s: An operator is a symbol or keyword that performs an operation on one or more values, called operands.

b.x: An operator is a symbol or keyword that performs an operation on one or more values, called operands. Python includes arithmetic, comparison, logical, bitwise, assignment, membership, and identity operators. The following sections focus on arithmetic, comparison, logical, and bitwise operators.

sec.s: Addition (+): 10 + 3 produces 13.

b.x: Addition (+): 10 + 3 produces 13. Subtraction (-): 10 - 3 produces 7. Multiplication (): 10 3 produces 30. Division (/): 10 / 3 produces approximately 3.3333333333333335. Floor division (//): 10 // 3 produces 3. Modulo (%): 10 % 3 produces 1. Exponentiation (): 2 3 produces 8. Unary minus (-x): reverses the sign of x. Unary plus (+x): keeps the sign of x.

Floor division rounds down toward negative infinity. Therefore, -10 // 3 produces -4, not -3. Modulo follows Python’s corresponding division rules. Modulo is often used to test divisibility: number % 2 == 0 checks whether an integer is even.
13.1 Order of operations
Python follows operator precedence. Multiplication, division, floor division, and modulo bind more tightly than addition and subtraction. Parentheses make the intended order clear:
Exponentiation has higher precedence than multiplication and addition. When an expression is difficult to read, use parentheses rather than relying on memory.
13.2 Division by zero
Ordinary division, floor division, or modulo by zero raises ZeroDivisionError. Validate a divisor if it may be zero.

b.x: Comparison operators compare values and generally return True or False.

Equal to (==): 5 == 5 is True. Not equal to (!=): 5 != 3 is True. Greater than (>): 7 > 4 is True. Less than (<): 2 < 8 is True. Greater than or equal to (>=): 5 >= 5 is True. Less than or equal to (<=): 3 <= 4 is True.
The single equals sign = assigns a value; == compares values.
Python supports chained comparisons

This checks that age is at least 18 and no greater than 60. String comparisons use Unicode code-point ordering and may not match language-aware dictionary order in every language. Specialized tools may be needed for culturally appropriate sorting.

b.x: 15.1 and
The expression A and B is truthy only when both operands are truthy. With Boolean operands, this is logical conjunction.
Both conditions must be true.
A or B is truthy when at least one operand is truthy.
The example runs if either condition is true.
15.3 not
not reverses a truth value

15.4 Truthiness and short-circuiting
Python conditions can use values beyond True and False. Empty strings, zero, None, and empty containers are falsey; many non-empty values are truthy.

and and or use short-circuit evaluation. In A and B, if A is falsey, Python need not evaluate B. In A or B, if A is truthy, Python need not evaluate B. These operators return one of their operands, not necessarily a literal Boolean, which matters when storing the result.

Truth table: A=False, B=False: A and B is False; A or B is False. A=False, B=True: A and B is False; A or B is True. A=True, B=False: A and B is False; A or B is True. A=True, B=True: A and B is True; A or B is True.

sec.s: A bit is a binary digit, 0 or 1.

b.x: 16.1 Bits

A bit is a binary digit, 0 or 1. Bitwise operators act on the binary representation of integer values. They are useful for flags, masks, low-level protocols, and some hardware-related operations. For ordinary conditions, logical operators are usually more appropriate.
16.2 Bitwise AND (&)
AND produces 1 at a bit position only when both corresponding bits are 1.
5 is 0101 in binary. 3 is 0011 in binary. 5 & 3 gives 0001, which is 1.
16.3 Bitwise OR (|)
OR produces 1 at a position when either corresponding bit is 1.
16.4 Bitwise XOR (^)
XOR produces 1 when corresponding bits differ.
16.5 Bitwise NOT (~)

Bitwise NOT inverts bits according to Python’s integer semantics. For Python integers, ~x equals -x - 1. Thus ~5 evaluates to -6. This may surprise learners familiar with fixed-width unsigned binary representations.
16.6 Left shift (<<)
A left shift moves bits left and fills low-order positions with zeros. For non-negative integers, shifting left by n places corresponds to multiplying by 2**n.
5 << 1 gives 10.
16.7 Right shift (>>)
A right shift moves bits to the right. For non-negative integers, shifting right by n places corresponds to floor division by 2**n.
8 >> 1 gives 4.
16.8 Logical versus bitwise operators
Logical operators are and, or, and not. Bitwise operators are &, |, ^, ~, <<, and >>.

For example, 5 and 3 evaluates to 3 because both values are truthy and and returns the second operand. But 5 & 3 evaluates to 1 because it performs bitwise AND. Use the operator family that matches the intended task.

sec.s: Control structures determine the order in which statements execute.

b.x: Control structures determine the order in which statements execute. Without them, a simple program generally runs sequentially. Conditions allow decisions; loops repeat work.

The main structures here are if, elif, else, for, and while. break and continue affect loops, while pass acts as a placeholder. A colon at the end of a condition or loop header introduces an indented block. Four spaces per indentation level is the common style.

sec.s: A while loop repeats as long as its condition remains truthy.

b.x: 21.1 Meaning
A while loop repeats as long as its condition remains truthy. It is useful when the number of repetitions depends on a condition rather than a predetermined sequence.
This prints 1 through 5. The update count += 1 is important because it moves the condition toward becoming false.
21.2 Infinite loops
If a while condition never becomes false and the loop never exits, the program may run indefinitely.
This is a problematic loop because count never changes. The condition remains true until the program is interrupted externally.

21.4 for versus while

Use for when iterating over a sequence or range. Use while when repetition should continue until a condition changes. Both can sometimes solve the same task; choose the structure that makes the intent easiest to understand.

sec.s: A nested loop is a loop inside another loop.

b.x: 22.1 Meaning
A nested loop is a loop inside another loop. For every iteration of the outer loop, the inner loop runs according to its own range or collection.
The outer loop runs three times and the inner loop runs twice for each outer iteration, so six pairs are printed.
22.2 Number of iterations

If the outer loop runs m times and the inner loop runs n times for every outer iteration, the inner statement generally executes m × n times. Three outer iterations and four inner iterations produce twelve inner executions.
Nested loops are useful for small tables and matrices, but their work can grow quickly as input sizes increase.
22.3 Printing a rectangle
The inner loop prints four stars. The print() after the inner loop starts a new line. The result is three rows of four stars.
22.4 Triangle pattern
Output
The number of stars depends on the row number.
22.5 Processing a matrix
The outer loop selects each row and the inner loop processes the values in that row.
22.6 Common nested-loop errors
Indentation controls which statements belong to which loop. If print() is indented inside the inner loop instead of after it, the output formatting changes.
Avoid reusing the same loop variable name for both loops. For example, using i for both the outer and inner loops can make the logic confusing. Names such as row and column are clearer.

sec.s: break immediately exits the nearest enclosing loop.

b.x: 23.1 break
break immediately exits the nearest enclosing loop.
Output: 1 2 3 4
When number becomes 5, the loop ends. break is useful when a search finds the desired item or when a condition requires the loop to stop.
23.2 continue
continue skips the remainder of the current iteration and moves to the next iteration of the nearest enclosing loop.
Output: 1 2 4 5
The value 3 is skipped, but the loop continues.
23.3 pass
pass performs no operation. It is a placeholder used where Python syntax requires a statement but the implementation has not yet been written.
This is syntactically valid and does nothing. pass does not exit the loop or skip to the next iteration; execution simply proceeds to the next statement.
23.4 Comparison
break: Ends the nearest enclosing loop immediately. continue: Skips the remainder of the current iteration and starts the next iteration. pass: Does nothing and allows normal execution to continue.
23.5 break in a while loop
The loop ends when attempts reaches 3, so only attempts 1 and 2 are printed.
23.6 continue to filter values
Even numbers are skipped, so the odd numbers from 1 through 9 are printed.
23.7 pass as a placeholder

The function is syntactically valid but does not calculate anything. It is useful temporarily during development. In finished software, replace placeholder code with the intended behavior or explicitly report that the operation is unsupported.

sec.s: Syntax errors occur when code does not follow Python grammar, such as missing colons or unmatched parentheses.

b.x: Syntax errors occur when code does not follow Python grammar, such as missing colons or unmatched parentheses.
Indentation errors occur when blocks are not indented consistently. Four spaces per indentation level is the common style.
Type errors occur when an operation is not supported for the supplied types. For example, “age:” + 18 raises TypeError. Use str(18) or an f-string.
Value errors occur when a value has the right general type for an operation but an invalid format. int(“hello”) raises ValueError.
Name errors occur when code uses a name that has not been defined. Check spelling and assignment order.
Infinite loops can happen when a while condition never becomes false. Make sure there is a clear update or exit path.
Off-by-one errors are common because range() excludes its stop value. To print 1 through 5, use range(1, 6), not range(1, 5).
Use descriptive names such as total_price instead of tp when meaning matters. Avoid reusing built-in names such as list or sum.
Run short programs and inspect outputs. When a result is unexpected, check variable values and condition results rather than changing many lines at once.
Comments begin with # and are ignored by Python. Use comments to explain why a decision is made, especially when the reason is not obvious.

sec.s: Revision recap

b.x: Python is a high-level, general-purpose programming language created by Guido van Rossum and first released publicly in 1991. Python 3 is the modern standard generation. Its readable syntax, standard library, cross-platform support, and package ecosystem make it useful in web development, automation, data analysis, and AI.

A Python environment includes an interpreter, editor or IDE, terminal, and sometimes pip and a virtual environment. pip installs third-party packages. Virtual environments isolate project dependencies.

Variables are names that refer to objects. The core types in this chapter are int, float, str, and bool. Type conversion uses functions such as int(), float(), str(), and bool(). Operators perform arithmetic, comparisons, logical combinations, and bitwise operations.

Control structures determine program flow. if, elif, and else select blocks based on conditions. for loops iterate over sequences; while loops repeat while a condition is true; nested loops place one loop inside another. break exits a loop, continue skips the rest of an iteration, and pass performs no operation.
